transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-05-14
Time: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 46 minutes
Location: Zoom
Attendees: Jenna Morales (Redwood AE), Arjun Patel (Redwood SE), Maya Chen (Aurora ML), Tom Rivera (Aurora SRE), Dr. Leo Park (Product), Sara Lim (Eng Manager)

[00:00] Jenna: okay folks, thanks for taking the time. quick agenda — align on what success looks like for the POC, agree SLO definitions (TTFT vs TPOT), sizing and sampling plan for benchmarks, and map next 3 weeks.
[00:18] Maya: sounds good, want to make sure we set targets that reflect our interactive use — mostly clinical note summarization via chat and some batch embeddings for search.
[00:29] Arjun: great, before we dive TTFT/TPOT, can you give a quick refresh on current stack and traffic? like p50 prompt length, tokens per response, and concurrency peaks.
[00:40] Sara: sure — our prod inference today is a mix. quick snapshot: median prompt ~45 tokens, median response ~120 tokens, spikes up to 512 tokens for full note generations. Concurrency: typical 30-50 QPS during peak, but some batch jobs push thousands of embeddings overnight.
[00:58] Tom: infra is AWS us-east-1, we keep customer data in our VPC. For pilot, we prefer hosted endpoints but need VPC peering / private link for egress.
[01:12] Jenna: noted. So high-level POC options: hosted API to iterate fast or dedicated/pinned nodes for controlled TTFT/TPOT — that'll influence acceptance.
[01:26] Dr. Leo: our main product KPI is interactive latency; if clinicians wait more than ~300ms to first token it disrupts flow. We also care about tail behavior p99 because that's what the report shows clinicians complain about.
[01:44] Arjun: good, that frames it. quick defs so we're aligned: TTFT = time-to-first-token (time from request accepted to first token emitted). TPOT (we use shorthand) = time-per-output-token or token throughput which maps to steady-state per-token latency; practically affects long responses.
[01:58] Maya: can you show an example acceptance matrix? like what are realistic p95/p99 numbers.
[02:05] Arjun: yes. For an interactive chat config with a medium model (open quantized 7B class) on GPU backends we typically see TTFT p95 around 120-220ms and p99 around 300-600ms depending on cold starts and kv cache state. TPOT p95 might be 8-20ms per token, p99 30-60ms per token. But that range depends on batching, sequence length, and kernel optimizations.
[02:35] Tom: those ranges are wide. we need concrete targets for our acceptance criteria. maybe start with conservative: p95 TTFT <=180ms, p99 <=450ms, TPOT p95 <=20ms/token for median responses (120 tokens) and p99 <=45ms/token.
[02:52] Jenna: makes sense as a starting point. We'll record those as proposed acceptance thresholds but plan to measure both cold and warm scenarios. Important: cold means no KV cache warm, warm = session with KV primed.
[03:08] Sara: how do you measure cold/warm? our production has session affinity so many flows are warm.
[03:13] Arjun: measurement plan: 1) warm runs using a seeded session history to prime KV cache; 2) cold runs by restarting process between requests or using a different user ID to ensure no shared cache; 3) ramp tests to simulate peaks; 4) sustained throughput tests to measure TPOT under load. We'll capture p50/p95/p99 for TTFT and per-token latency distributions.
[03:35] Maya: and what about batching? some of our prod paths batch on the client (we do small micro-batches). batching will change TPOT vs TTFT tradeoffs.
[03:44] Arjun: right — we plan tests with different client-side batch sizes: 1, 4, 8. Also test Redwood server-side batching config set to minimal (low-latency) and throughput-optimized. We'll include concurrency sweeps 1-200 to see queueing effects.
[04:02] Dr. Leo: can we include an 'unhappy path' like sudden spike causing fallback to a smaller model? we want the SLO to include graceful degradation behavior.
[04:12] Jenna: good call. We'll add a scenario to validate fallback policy: when CPU/GPU saturation hits X% or queue latency > Y ms, auto-fallback to a smaller model with preserved correctness. Acceptance should tolerate up to 1% of requests served by fallback during a 10-minute spike window but not exceed 5% sustained.
[04:35] Tom: on measurement tools, are you providing the load runner or do we run ours?
[04:39] Arjun: Redwood will deliver a reproducible workload generator (python-based) that supports your prompt corpus, session affinity toggles, variable token lengths, and network jitter injection. We'll version it in the repo and share instructions.
[04:55] Maya: perfect. can you also include instructions to reproduce in our test VPC? security will ask.
[04:59] Jenna: yes, we'll include deployment options: hosted with VPC peering or dedicated nodes in your VPC. For the pilot we recommend hosted with VPC peering to move faster.
[05:12] [05:12] — brief crosstalk about recruitment of SREs for peering window — [05:20]
[05:20] Arjun: returning to SLO metrics — we propose the POC acceptance matrix structure: workload type (interactive chat, long form, batch embed), traffic profile (normal/peak/spike), metric (TTFT p95/p99, TPOT p95/p99, error rate, tail CPU/GPU utilization), and pass/fail thresholds. We'll share a template sheet.
[05:38] Sara: can the sheet include cost estimates per million tokens for each model variant? budget will be reviewed by finance.
[05:44] Jenna: yes, we'll add estimated cost curves and expected instance footprints for Dedicated vs Hosted. That helps you decide capacity.
[05:52] Maya: what about evaluation windows? like how long should a run be to get stable p99 estimates?
[05:58] Arjun: for p99 you need decent sample sizes. rule of thumb: run sustained traffic for at least 20-30 minutes at target QPS, and repeat runs at least 3 times. For spike tests, do 10-minute bursts with pre and post baseline. We'll also collect kernel-level metrics to know if tails were due to GC, network, or contention.
[06:20] Tom: kernel-level metrics — we want logs for per-request latency and GPU utilization at 5s granularity. Is that available in Redwood Console?
[06:27] Jenna: yes, Console exposes token-level latency breakdown, trace sampling and per-route dashboards. For pilots we can give access to the trial dashboard.
[06:36] Dr. Leo: how do you handle variability from model randomness? e.g., some generations may be longer semiflur, does that skew TPOT measurements?
[06:45] Arjun: we use controlled sampling: fixed random seeds for generation where possible, and for non-deterministic tests we bucket token lengths and report TPOT normalized per token length. We'll include median token length cohorts (50, 120, 256, 512) so you can compare apples-to-apples.
[07:02] Maya: ok. any thoughts on p99 goal for long responses — our long-form p99 is most critical because those are multi-step summaries.
[07:09] Arjun: long-form tradeoffs — with 512 tokens, TPOT p95 might hold but p99 can balloon due to KV cache thrash. For acceptance we suggest long-form p95 <=30ms/token and p99 <=70ms/token for 512 token outputs on Dedicated nodes with warm cache. If hosted, slightly looser: p95 <=40ms/token p99 <=90ms/token.
[07:35] Sara: these look doable, but we need to understand what model families you'll test.
[07:40] Jenna: planned model variants: open 7B quant (4-bit), open 13B quant, and a small proprietary optimized model — we'll map each to expected TTFT/TPOT footprints. If you want to include Anthropic/Prod APIs for baseline, we can too.
[07:56] Tom: do you include tokenizer overhead in TTFT? our pipeline does some client-side preprocessing.
[08:02] Arjun: TTFT will be measured end-to-end from request ingress to first token at Redwood's API. Client-side preprocessing should be excluded; we can measure separate preproc times if you want.
[08:12] Maya: also can we measure tokenization differences — some tokenizers yield different token counts which impacts TPOT.
[08:18] Arjun: yes we'll instrument tokens per request and normalize. The sampling plan will annotate samples with tokenizer counts.
[08:25] [08:25] — short pause —
[08:30] Jenna: rough timeline proposal: week 0 (this week) — align on prompts and access; week 1 — Redwood builds workload generator + dry-run in hosted environment; week 2 — formal benchmark runs and data collection; week 3 — analysis and acceptance review. total ~3 weeks with opportunity to extend for Dedicated sizing.
[08:54] Maya: that timeline fits our release cadence. finance signoff by end of month.
[09:00] Dr. Leo: about acceptance, can we set both hard and soft SLOs? hard = must pass for go/no-go, soft = target for optimization.
[09:10] Arjun: yes. Example: hard SLO for interactive chat: TTFT p95 <=250ms (hard), p95 <=180ms (soft). TPOT hard p95 <=40ms/token, soft p95 <=20ms/token. We'll publish both in the matrix.
[09:28] Sara: error budget — how many infra errors acceptable during test?
[09:32] Jenna: propose 0.5% total error rate as hard threshold over 1-hour sustained run, and <=0.1% as soft target. We'll define error categories (5xx, timeouts, model errors) in the sheet.
[09:45] Tom: security/compliance notes: we need to validate SOC2 + encryption in transit and at rest. Also KMS integration if we do Private later.
[09:55] Jenna: we'll attach our security packet. For pilot hosted with VPC peering, we'll provide encrypted transit; KMS can be integrated for Dedicated/Private.
[10:06] Maya: ok, last bit — what are acceptance artifacts? what will you hand over after benching?
[10:11] Arjun: deliverables: benchmark raw logs (CSV), aggregated SLO report with p50/p95/p99, cost projection sheet, configuration manifests used (model + batch + kernel flags), and a playbook for repro. We'll also include a short recommendations doc for quantization/batching settings.
[10:29] Jenna: thanks. Any other questions from the team?
[10:33] Maya: one more — in the measurement plan, can you include a probe to detect GC pauses or host swap events? we've seen that bite us before.
[10:40] Arjun: yes, we'll include host-level metrics and correlation traces to identify GC or memory spikes. We'll also record tail stack traces when available.
[10:48] Tom: what about load shaping? we'd like to replicate our diurnal ramp and also bursty patterns from web clients.
[10:54] Arjun: load runner supports traffic shaping: steady-state, sawtooth, and poisson bursts at configured percentiles. We'll include your real-world traffic profiles.
[11:03] Sara: for the fallback model test, how will you measure quality delta? our clinicians can't tolerate major hallucinations.
[11:09] Arjun: good point — we'll include a small eval set of ground-truth summaries and run automatic quality checks (ROUGE/BLEU analogs) and a manual sanity check for 30 samples pre/post fallback. Acceptance will require no more than X% degradation in key metrics — we can set that number with you.
[11:27] Maya: can you put a proposal for that X? maybe max 5% drop in summary accuracy for fallback.
[11:32] Jenna: we'll propose 5% as initial and you can tighten.
[11:35] [11:35] — wrap-up —
[11:36] Jenna: recap and next steps: Arjun builds the workload generator + sampling plan; Maya to provide prompt corpus; Jenna shares sec docs and pricing; schedule benchmark run week of 5/25. I'll put all this in the sheet and send calendar invites for the bench.
[11:53] Maya: thanks everyone. excited to get started.
[11:56] Jenna: thanks all — end.

Notes on transcription: occasional filler and mis-hearings corrected minimally — e.g., "K-V cash" appears transcribed once for KV cache. Names may be slightly off.
